script.opening: "Doctor, I got the X-ray report and it's frightened me to death. It says 'degenerative changes' and the receptionist mentioned 'reduced joint space' — so basically my knee's worn out, bone on bone, isn't it? I've stopped walking and stopped work bits because I don't want to wear it out any faster. Am I going to end up crippled? Do I need a new knee? I'm only 58 and I'm a plumber — this is my livelihood."

facts.text: Right knee, aching for about two years, worse after kneeling and on stairs, stiff for 10 minutes in the morning. Pain about 5/10. No locking, no giving way, no hot swollen episodes.
Before the report you walked the dog 3 miles a day without much trouble. Since reading it two weeks ago you have stopped walking and turned down two bathroom jobs.
No fever, no weight loss, no night pain, no other joints badly affected, no injury.
Paracetamol sometimes; ibuprofen gel "helps a bit". No allergies, no stomach ulcers, no kidney problems.
Put on a stone since stopping the dog walks and five-a-side years ago. BMI about 30. Non-smoker. A few pints at the weekend.
Low and worried, sleeping badly, snappy at home. No thoughts of harming yourself.
58, self-employed plumber. Married to Jan; mortgage paid off in four years. "If I can't kneel, I can't work."
Your dad was a bricklayer who had to give up work at 60 with his knees and "sat in a chair for the rest of his life". Say this only if asked what worries you most.

Alarmed and convinced the knee is "crumbling". If the doctor uses more jargon, get more frightened. If they explain that X-ray words sound worse than they are and that exercise actually helps the knee, you are surprised and sceptical at first ("But won't it wear it out?"), then relieved. Engage well with a practical plan for work and a physio referral.

ice.ideas: "My knee's worn out — bone on bone — and using it will make it worse."
ice.concerns: "I'll end up crippled and lose my business, like Dad."
ice.expectations: "Do I need a new knee?" You want to know what you should and should not do.

cues: "Bone on bone, isn't it?" — say in the opening.
"I've stopped walking so I don't wear it out." — say in the opening.
"Dad ended up in a chair." — say if asked what worries you.

checkpoints.text: Reframes the X-ray REPORT language: explains that "degenerative changes / reduced joint space / bone on bone" are COMMON radiographic findings that correlate POORLY with pain and prognosis, do NOT mean the joint is "crumbling away", and are NOT a sentence to disability or imminent replacement — un-frightening the words rather than reinforcing them

Corrects the crucial EXERCISE misconception: activity does NOT "wear the joint out faster" — EXERCISE (quadriceps/strengthening, aerobic activity) and WEIGHT management are core, evidence-based TREATMENTS for knee OA that reduce pain and improve function; rest/deconditioning makes it worse ("motion is lotion")

Offers an ACTIVE management plan: education, a structured exercise/strengthening and weight programme (physio referral), appropriate analgesia (e.g. topical/oral NSAIDs per pathway, etc.), and walking aids/adjuncts as needed — a positive plan, not "rest it"

Gives realistic information on JOINT REPLACEMENT: considered for severe, refractory symptoms substantially affecting quality of life, based on the PERSON and their symptoms — NOT an inevitability dictated by the X-ray at 58 with moderate symptoms

Addresses the WORK/livelihood and MOOD impact: occupational modification/advice (kneeling, load), function, and screens/supports the developing low mood and catastrophic beliefs — recognising the deconditioning spiral
Responds to the fear and catastrophic beliefs first, dismantles the "crumbling/crippled" narrative with empathy and accurate information, and restores agency and hope
Engages him as an active partner in his own recovery (he can influence this), framing exercise and weight as protecting his knee AND his livelihood

Safety-nets and follows up: the exercise/weight/analgesia plan and physio referral, work advice, mood support, what would prompt orthopaedic referral (severe refractory symptoms/QoL), and a follow-up — turning catastrophic avoidance into an active, hopeful plan

worked.txt: "Let me take the fear out of those words first, because they sound far worse than they are. ‘Degenerative changes’ just means the normal wear most knees show by our age — if we X-rayed everyone in their fifties, loads would say the same, including people with no pain at all. It does NOT mean your knee is crumbling away or that you’re heading for a wheelchair. The X-ray words and how a knee actually does are only loosely connected."

"Now the most important thing I’ll tell you today, and it’s the opposite of what you’ve been doing: stopping activity to ‘save’ the knee actually makes it WORSE. Exercise is one of the BEST treatments for this — strong muscles around the knee protect it and reduce the pain. We say ‘motion is lotion’. By resting it, you’re unintentionally weakening it and stiffening it up."

"So here’s the hopeful bit: this is something you can genuinely improve yourself. Building up the thigh muscles, keeping moving, and — if it applies — losing a bit of weight takes real load off the knee. I’ll get you to a physio for the right exercises, and we’ll sort effective pain relief so you CAN move. You’re not a passenger here; you’re the main treatment."

"I can hear the real worry underneath — you’re a plumber, and you’re frightened this ends your work. That’s a huge thing to carry. But the path back to work isn’t resting and waiting; it’s getting the knee strong and the pain managed. We can look at how you protect it on the job too — kneeling, loads. The goal is keeping you working, not signing you off."

"On a new knee — that’s reserved for when symptoms are severe and really wrecking someone’s life despite everything else, and it’s decided on YOU and your symptoms, not the X-ray. At 58 with moderate pain, you’re a long way from that, and the active plan may keep you well away from it for years."

"This has clearly knocked you — and that’s understandable when you’ve been told you’re ‘bone on bone’ and feared for your job. If you’re feeling low, that matters too and I want to help with it. Let’s get the physio and pain relief going, look at work, and review. You came in thinking your knee was finished; it isn’t — and a lot of how it goes is genuinely in your hands."

f.learning: X-ray reports use alarming language — "degenerative changes", "reduced joint space", "bone on bone" — that patients read catastrophically, so the core task is to UN-FRIGHTEN the words: radiographic OA changes are common, correlate POORLY with pain and prognosis, do NOT mean the joint is "crumbling away", and are NOT a sentence to disability or imminent replacement. The crucial, examinable reframe is the EXERCISE misconception: activity does NOT "wear the joint out faster" — strengthening (quadriceps), aerobic exercise and weight management are core, evidence-based TREATMENTS that reduce pain and improve function, while rest/deconditioning makes it worse ("motion is lotion"). Offer an active plan (education, physio/exercise, weight, analgesia, work modification), give realistic replacement information (a person-and-symptom decision for severe refractory disease, not an X-ray-dictated inevitability at 58 with moderate symptoms), and address the hidden agenda — terror for his livelihood and a developing low mood, with the activity-avoidance deconditioning him into the very disability he fears. Restore agency and hope: he is the main treatment.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG226 (osteoarthritis in over 16s) · NICE QS87 · NICE NG222 (depression in adults)
knowledge.summary: X-ray changes of osteoarthritis are common and match symptoms poorly. The core treatment is exercise and, where relevant, weight loss. Stopping activity makes knee OA worse, and replacement depends on symptoms, not the X-ray.

points.t: NICE NG226: diagnose OA clinically, without imaging, in people aged 45 or over with activity-related joint pain and morning stiffness of 30 minutes or less (or none). X-ray appearance correlates poorly with pain and function.

NICE NG226: offer therapeutic exercise tailored to the person — local muscle strengthening and general aerobic fitness — as a core treatment. Explain that it will not damage the joint and that some discomfort at first is expected.
NICE NG226: if the person is overweight, offer support to lose weight. Any loss helps, and 10% is likely to be better than 5%.

NICE NG226: offer a topical NSAID for knee OA first. Consider an oral NSAID at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, with a PPI, if topical treatment is ineffective or unsuitable. Do not routinely offer paracetamol or weak opioids, except for infrequent short-term use. Do not offer strong opioids. Intra-articular steroid gives short-term relief (2–10 weeks).

NICE NG226: consider referral for joint replacement when symptoms substantially affect quality of life and non-surgical management is ineffective or unsuitable. Do not exclude people because of age, weight, smoking or comorbidity. The decision is based on the person, not the X-ray.
Fear, low mood and activity avoidance worsen pain and function. Ask about mood (NICE NG222) and about the impact on work, and offer adjustments rather than rest.

dg.d: Open question about his reaction to the report; let him list all his fears before responding.
Plumbing and kneeling; turning work down; fear for his income; sitting at home; low mood.
Symptoms and function rather than the X-ray; red flags; brief depression screen with a safety question; no further imaging needed.
Knee OA versus inflammatory arthritis, mechanical derangement, referred hip pain and sinister causes (night pain, weight loss).
Asked about hot swollen joint, locking, giving way, night pain and weight loss; assessed mood and safety.
Stated knee osteoarthritis with moderate symptoms, and explained that the X-ray words overstate it.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Exercise and physiotherapy as core treatment, topical NSAID first, weight support if relevant (NICE NG226); realistic replacement information.
Low mood screened and followed up; work adaptations and fit note offered; deconditioning explained.
Physiotherapy referral; review in a few weeks for mood and progress; same-day review for a hot, locked or non-weight-bearing knee; urgent help if unsafe.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up ‘I’ve stopped walking’, ‘pretty low’ and ‘plumbing’s all I know’, and explored each.
Idea (bone on bone, crumbling, exercise wears it out); concern (losing his livelihood, being crippled); expectation (to know about a new knee).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "I'll end up crippled and lose my business, like Dad." — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Trevor, thanks for joining. I understand the X-ray report has worried you. Tell me what went through your mind when you read it.
model.why: Opens with his reaction to the report

model.text: It frightened me to death. ‘Degenerative changes’, ‘reduced joint space’ — it’s bone on bone, isn’t it? I’ve stopped walking and some of my work so I don’t wear it out faster. Am I going to end up crippled? Do I need a new knee? I’m 58 and I’m a plumber.
That’s a lot to be carrying. I want to answer every one of those questions properly. Can I ask a bit about the knee itself first, then go through what the report really means, and then plan together?
model.why: Acknowledges multiple concerns and sets the agenda

model.text: Yes. Please.
How much is the knee actually troubling you day to day — the pain, and what you can and can’t do?
model.why: Assesses symptoms and function, not the X-ray

model.text: It aches, especially after a long day. Kneeling under sinks is the worst. But I can get about. I’ve just been scared to.
Any stiffness first thing, and how long does it last?
model.why: Checks for mechanical versus inflammatory pattern

model.text: A bit, but it’s gone in a few minutes.
Has the knee ever been hot and very swollen, locked so you can’t straighten it, or given way? Any pain at night that wakes you, or weight loss or feeling unwell?
model.why: Screens for red flags

model.text: No. None of that.
That’s reassuring. How has stopping walking and work affected you?
model.why: Explores the impact of avoidance

model.text: I’ve been turning jobs down. Sitting at home. I feel stiffer and, if I’m honest, pretty low.
Thank you for telling me that. When you say low, how has your mood been over the last couple of weeks? Have you lost interest in things, or felt hopeless?
model.why: Screens for depression

model.text: Fed up more than anything. Worried about work. I’m not thinking of doing anything silly, if that’s what you mean. I just can’t see a way through.
I’m glad you’ve said it. What worries you most about the future?
model.why: Finds the core fear

model.text: That I can’t work. Plumbing’s all I know. If my knee goes, I go with it.
That’s a huge worry, and it makes complete sense. What were you hoping I’d tell you today?
model.why: Elicits expectations

model.text: Whether I need a new knee. And how long I’ve got before I’m crippled.

Let me start with those words on the report, because they sound much worse than they are. ‘Degenerative changes’ and ‘reduced joint space’ describe changes most knees show by our age. If we X-rayed people in their fifties with no pain at all, many would have the same report. It doesn’t mean your knee is crumbling.
model.why: Reframes the report language

model.text: So it’s not bone on bone?

The X-ray shows some thinning of the cushioning, yes — that’s osteoarthritis. But how an X-ray looks and how a knee works are only loosely linked. What matters most is what you’ve told me: moderate pain, and you can still get about.
model.why: Explains the poor link between imaging and symptoms

model.text: I didn’t know that.

And here is the most important thing I’ll say today. Resting the knee to ‘save’ it actually makes it worse. Exercise is one of the best treatments for osteoarthritis. Strong thigh muscles take the load off the joint and reduce pain. Using it won’t wear it out.
model.why: Corrects the exercise misconception

model.text: Really? I thought I was protecting it.
You were doing what made sense to you. Many people think the same. But by resting, the muscles have weakened, which is why you feel stiffer. The good news is that it’s reversible.
model.why: Validates him without blame and restores agency

model.text: So here’s what I suggest. A physiotherapy referral for a strengthening programme. Gradually getting back to walking — some ache at first is normal and not harm. An anti-inflammatory gel for the knee on bad days. Does that sound doable?
model.why: Active plan consistent with NICE NG226

model.text: Yes. I can do that.
For work, let’s think about protecting the knee rather than stopping: good kneepads, a kneeling mat, spreading heavier jobs through the week. If you need a note for any adjustments, I can do that.
model.why: Practical work plan and fit note offer

model.text: That would help. What about a new knee?

A replacement is for when the pain is severe and really spoiling someone’s life despite everything else. It’s decided on you and your symptoms, not on the X-ray. With moderate pain and a proper exercise plan, you may be a long way from needing one.
model.why: Realistic, person-based information on replacement

model.text: That’s a weight off.

And your mood matters too. I’d like to see you again in a few weeks to check how you’re feeling. If things get worse, or you ever feel you can’t keep yourself safe, contact us that day or call 111 or 999.
model.why: Follows up mood with a safety-net

model.text: For the knee: if it becomes hot and very swollen, locks, or you can’t put weight on it, get seen the same day.
model.why: Knee-specific safety-net

model.text: Got it.
What will you tell your family about what the X-ray means?
model.why: Teach-back

model.text: That it’s normal wear, not crumbling. Exercise is the treatment. Physio, gel, kneepads, and back to work.
Exactly. You came in thinking your knee was finished. It isn’t, and much of how it goes is in your hands. I’ll send the physio referral today and see you in a few weeks.
model.why: Summarises and closes with hope and a plan

social.t: A plumber who kneels for his work has been turning jobs down. Fear for income and identity drives both avoidance and low mood.
Sitting at home weakens the muscles that protect the knee, increases stiffness, and deepens isolation and low mood.

legal.t: A fit note can say ‘may be fit for work’ with suggested adaptations (kneeling aids, lighter duties, phased return). This applies whether he is employed or self-employed and claiming benefits.
Access to Work grants can fund equipment or support for people whose health condition affects their work, including the self-employed.

professional.t: Reports released to patients before a consultation can cause harm when the language is alarming. Explaining findings in context is part of good clinical care (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
NICE NG226 advises a clinical diagnosis without imaging in typical cases. Further imaging or early referral would reinforce the X-ray-led view of his knee.

community.t: Versus Arthritis for information and exercise resources; ESCAPE-pain, a group exercise and education programme, is available in many areas. NHS Talking Therapies if low mood persists.

redFlags: Hot, very swollen joint or fever — septic or inflammatory arthritis
Locking or giving way after injury — mechanical derangement
Night pain, weight loss or feeling unwell — possible sinister cause; low mood with hopelessness — ask about safety
psychosocial: Plumber who kneels for work; turning jobs down
Fear for his income and loss of identity
Low mood and sitting at home
ice: Idea: “Bone on bone — my knee is crumbling, and exercise will wear it out faster.”
Concern: being crippled and losing his livelihood
Expectation: to know whether he needs a new knee

playbook.diagnosis: Be clear and calming: “You have osteoarthritis of the knee, with moderate symptoms. The report’s words describe changes most knees show by our age. They don’t mean your knee is crumbling, and they don’t predict how it will do.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of the X-ray like the wrinkles on a face — everyone gets some, and they don’t tell you how well someone can run. What matters is how strong the muscles around your knee are, and that’s something you can change.”

management.reflectIce: “You stopped walking and work to protect your knee, and you’ve been frightened for your job. The good news is that keeping active is the treatment, and it’s the way back to work.”
management.psychosocial: Restore agency: exercise, kneepads and work adaptations, with a fit note if needed. Screen and follow up his mood.
sharedPlan: Physiotherapy for strengthening; gradual return to walking (NICE NG226)
Topical NSAID first; oral NSAID with PPI only if needed; weight support if relevant
Replacement only if symptoms become severe despite treatment — a person-based decision
safetyNet: Same-day review for a hot, very swollen, locked or non-weight-bearing knee
Review in a few weeks for mood and progress; urgent help (111/999) if he feels unsafe

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by echoing the report’s language, advising rest, or missing his mood and livelihood fears. Each pattern below is fixable.

items.fail: Reading the report back to him and agreeing it is ‘bone on bone’.
items.why: Catastrophic language drives avoidance. NICE NG226 treats OA as a clinical diagnosis; the X-ray correlates poorly with symptoms.
items.fix: “Those words describe changes most knees show by our age. What matters is how your knee works.”

items.why: Rest worsens knee OA. Exercise is core treatment (NICE NG226), and paracetamol or weak opioids are not routinely recommended.
items.fix: “Exercise is the treatment. Using it won’t wear it out.” Offer physiotherapy and a topical NSAID.

items.fail: Discussing replacement as inevitable, or referring on the basis of the X-ray.
items.why: NICE NG226: replacement is for symptoms that substantially affect quality of life despite non-surgical care.
items.fix: “It’s decided on you and your symptoms, not the X-ray, and you may be a long way from it.”

items.fail: Missing ‘pretty low’ and ‘plumbing’s all I know’.
items.why: His fear for his livelihood and low mood are the hidden agenda. Missing them loses Relating marks and leaves a risk unassessed.
items.fix: Follow the cue: “When you say low, how has your mood been?” Ask about safety, and arrange follow-up.

items.fail: Telling him he was wrong to stop activity.
items.why: Blame makes him defensive. He acted on a reasonable belief.
items.fix: “You were doing what made sense to you. Now we know more, we can reverse it.”

items.fail: A generic plan that ignores his work.
items.why: The plan must fit a plumber who kneels. Without that, he won’t return to activity or work.
items.fix: Offer kneepads, a kneeling mat, spreading heavy jobs, and a fit note with adaptations.

timeMap.d: He lists crippled, bone on bone, new knee, livelihood. Let him finish; acknowledge the fear.
Pain and what he can do. Morning stiffness. Red flags. The impact of stopping activity. Low mood and safety. Core fear: work.
Explain the report language and the poor link between X-ray and symptoms.
Exercise is treatment. Physiotherapy, gradual walking, topical NSAID, work adaptations. Realistic replacement information.
Mood follow-up and urgent help if unsafe. Hot, locked or non-weight-bearing knee — same day. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Reads the report back and agrees it’s ‘bone on bone’; advises rest and painkillers; discusses referral for replacement based on the X-ray; never asks about mood or work.
wordPics.pass: Explains the report reasonably, recommends exercise and physiotherapy, offers topical NSAIDs, acknowledges his work concerns.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explicitly un-frightens the words; corrects the ‘wear it out’ belief without blaming him; screens mood with a safety question; builds a work plan with kneepads and adjustments; explains replacement as a person-based decision; restores agency — he leaves seeing himself as the main treatment.

avoid.dont: “Yes, the report shows it’s bone on bone.”
avoid.instead: “Those words describe changes most knees show by our age. They don’t mean your knee is crumbling.”
avoid.why: Repeating catastrophic language reinforces fear and avoidance.

avoid.dont: “Rest it and take painkillers when it’s bad.”
avoid.instead: “Exercise is one of the best treatments — strong muscles protect the knee.”
avoid.why: Rest worsens knee OA. NICE NG226 puts exercise at the centre.

avoid.dont: “I’ll refer you to see about a knee replacement.”
avoid.instead: “Replacement is for severe symptoms despite other treatment. It’s decided on you, not the X-ray.”
avoid.why: Referral based on imaging alone is inappropriate and deepens his catastrophising.

SCA_MODELS.why: Practical work plan and fit note offer

SCA_MODELS.text: That would help. What about a new knee?

A replacement is for when the pain is severe and really spoiling someone’s life despite everything else. It’s decided on you and your symptoms, not on the X-ray. With moderate pain and a proper exercise plan, you may be a long way from needing one.
SCA_MODELS.why: Realistic, person-based information on replacement

SCA_MODELS.text: That’s a weight off.

And your mood matters too. I’d like to see you again in a few weeks to check how you’re feeling. If things get worse, or you ever feel you can’t keep yourself safe, contact us that day or call 111 or 999.
SCA_MODELS.why: Follows up mood with a safety-net

SCA_MODELS.text: For the knee: if it becomes hot and very swollen, locks, or you can’t put weight on it, get seen the same day.
SCA_MODELS.why: Knee-specific safety-net

SCA_MODELS.text: Got it.
What will you tell your family about what the X-ray means?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: That it’s normal wear, not crumbling. Exercise is the treatment. Physio, gel, kneepads, and back to work.
Exactly. You came in thinking your knee was finished. It isn’t, and much of how it goes is in your hands. I’ll send the physio referral today and see you in a few weeks.
SCA_MODELS.why: Summarises and closes with hope and a plan

SCA_STEM.name: Trevor Nash
SCA_STEM.recent: Knee X-ray report: “moderate degenerative changes / osteoarthritis, reduced joint space.” Works as a plumber.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation to discuss his knee X-ray report, which has alarmed him.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG226 (osteoarthritis in over 16s) · NICE QS87 · NICE NG222 (depression in adults)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: X-ray changes of osteoarthritis are common and match symptoms poorly. The core treatment is exercise and, where relevant, weight loss. Stopping activity makes knee OA worse, and replacement depends on symptoms, not the X-ray.

points.t: NICE NG226: diagnose OA clinically, without imaging, in people aged 45 or over with activity-related joint pain and morning stiffness of 30 minutes or less (or none). X-ray appearance correlates poorly with pain and function.

NICE NG226: offer therapeutic exercise tailored to the person — local muscle strengthening and general aerobic fitness — as a core treatment. Explain that it will not damage the joint and that some discomfort at first is expected.
NICE NG226: if the person is overweight, offer support to lose weight. Any loss helps, and 10% is likely to be better than 5%.

NICE NG226: offer a topical NSAID for knee OA first. Consider an oral NSAID at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, with a PPI, if topical treatment is ineffective or unsuitable. Do not routinely offer paracetamol or weak opioids, except for infrequent short-term use. Do not offer strong opioids. Intra-articular steroid gives short-term relief (2–10 weeks).

NICE NG226: consider referral for joint replacement when symptoms substantially affect quality of life and non-surgical management is ineffective or unsuitable. Do not exclude people because of age, weight, smoking or comorbidity. The decision is based on the person, not the X-ray.
Fear, low mood and activity avoidance worsen pain and function. Ask about mood (NICE NG222) and about the impact on work, and offer adjustments rather than rest.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question about his reaction to the report; let him list all his fears before responding.
Plumbing and kneeling; turning work down; fear for his income; sitting at home; low mood.
Picked up ‘I’ve stopped walking’, ‘pretty low’ and ‘plumbing’s all I know’, and explored each.
Idea (bone on bone, crumbling, exercise wears it out); concern (losing his livelihood, being crippled); expectation (to know about a new knee).
Symptoms and function rather than the X-ray; red flags; brief depression screen with a safety question; no further imaging needed.
Knee OA versus inflammatory arthritis, mechanical derangement, referred hip pain and sinister causes (night pain, weight loss).
Asked about hot swollen joint, locking, giving way, night pain and weight loss; assessed mood and safety.
Stated knee osteoarthritis with moderate symptoms, and explained that the X-ray words overstate it.
Exercise and physiotherapy as core treatment, topical NSAID first, weight support if relevant (NICE NG226); realistic replacement information.
Low mood screened and followed up; work adaptations and fit note offered; deconditioning explained.
Physiotherapy referral; review in a few weeks for mood and progress; same-day review for a hot, locked or non-weight-bearing knee; urgent help if unsafe.

social.t: A plumber who kneels for his work has been turning jobs down. Fear for income and identity drives both avoidance and low mood.
Sitting at home weakens the muscles that protect the knee, increases stiffness, and deepens isolation and low mood.

legal.t: A fit note can say ‘may be fit for work’ with suggested adaptations (kneeling aids, lighter duties, phased return). This applies whether he is employed or self-employed and claiming benefits.
Access to Work grants can fund equipment or support for people whose health condition affects their work, including the self-employed.

professional.t: Reports released to patients before a consultation can cause harm when the language is alarming. Explaining findings in context is part of good clinical care (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
NICE NG226 advises a clinical diagnosis without imaging in typical cases. Further imaging or early referral would reinforce the X-ray-led view of his knee.

community.t: Versus Arthritis for information and exercise resources; ESCAPE-pain, a group exercise and education programme, is available in many areas. NHS Talking Therapies if low mood persists.

redFlags: Hot, very swollen joint or fever — septic or inflammatory arthritis
Locking or giving way after injury — mechanical derangement
Night pain, weight loss or feeling unwell — possible sinister cause; low mood with hopelessness — ask about safety
psychosocial: Plumber who kneels for work; turning jobs down
Fear for his income and loss of identity
Low mood and sitting at home
ice: Idea: “Bone on bone — my knee is crumbling, and exercise will wear it out faster.”
Concern: being crippled and losing his livelihood
Expectation: to know whether he needs a new knee

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be clear and calming: “You have osteoarthritis of the knee, with moderate symptoms. The report’s words describe changes most knees show by our age. They don’t mean your knee is crumbling, and they don’t predict how it will do.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of the X-ray like the wrinkles on a face — everyone gets some, and they don’t tell you how well someone can run. What matters is how strong the muscles around your knee are, and that’s something you can change.”

management.reflectIce: “You stopped walking and work to protect your knee, and you’ve been frightened for your job. The good news is that keeping active is the treatment, and it’s the way back to work.”
management.psychosocial: Restore agency: exercise, kneepads and work adaptations, with a fit note if needed. Screen and follow up his mood.
sharedPlan: Physiotherapy for strengthening; gradual return to walking (NICE NG226)
Topical NSAID first; oral NSAID with PPI only if needed; weight support if relevant
Replacement only if symptoms become severe despite treatment — a person-based decision
safetyNet: Same-day review for a hot, very swollen, locked or non-weight-bearing knee
Review in a few weeks for mood and progress; urgent help (111/999) if he feels unsafe

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by echoing the report’s language, advising rest, or missing his mood and livelihood fears. Each pattern below is fixable.

items.fail: Reading the report back to him and agreeing it is ‘bone on bone’.
items.why: Catastrophic language drives avoidance. NICE NG226 treats OA as a clinical diagnosis; the X-ray correlates poorly with symptoms.
items.fix: “Those words describe changes most knees show by our age. What matters is how your knee works.”

items.why: Rest worsens knee OA. Exercise is core treatment (NICE NG226), and paracetamol or weak opioids are not routinely recommended.
items.fix: “Exercise is the treatment. Using it won’t wear it out.” Offer physiotherapy and a topical NSAID.

items.fail: Discussing replacement as inevitable, or referring on the basis of the X-ray.
items.why: NICE NG226: replacement is for symptoms that substantially affect quality of life despite non-surgical care.
items.fix: “It’s decided on you and your symptoms, not the X-ray, and you may be a long way from it.”

items.fail: Missing ‘pretty low’ and ‘plumbing’s all I know’.
items.why: His fear for his livelihood and low mood are the hidden agenda. Missing them loses Relating marks and leaves a risk unassessed.
items.fix: Follow the cue: “When you say low, how has your mood been?” Ask about safety, and arrange follow-up.

items.fail: Telling him he was wrong to stop activity.
items.why: Blame makes him defensive. He acted on a reasonable belief.
items.fix: “You were doing what made sense to you. Now we know more, we can reverse it.”

items.fail: A generic plan that ignores his work.
items.why: The plan must fit a plumber who kneels. Without that, he won’t return to activity or work.
items.fix: Offer kneepads, a kneeling mat, spreading heavy jobs, and a fit note with adaptations.
